races.long_description: Representative Barry Moore, a third-term Republican and longtime Trump loyalist, is running for the Senate seat being vacated by Tommy Tuberville, who is running for governor. Mr. Moore’s Democratic opponent, Everett Wess, a former judge and lawyer, is a long shot in deep-red Alabama.

Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, is trying to hold on to his seat against former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat. The wild card in the four-person ranked-choice race is the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan, a retiree in a small fishing village who has the same name as the incumbent.
Senator Tom Cotton, a Trump ally and the third-ranking Republican in the chamber, is heavily favored to win a third term. He is facing Hallie Shoffner, a Democrat and sixth-generation farmer.

Senator John Hickenlooper, a moderate incumbent, is running for a second term in a solidly Democratic seat. He faces Mark Baisley, a Republican state senator, and Bob Chew, a Navy veteran and former Republican who is running as an independent.

Senator Chris Coons, a Democrat, is heavily favored to win re-election in a state that Kamala Harris carried by about 15 percentage points two years ago. His Republican challenger is Mike Katz, a doctor who has served in Delaware’s State Senate.

Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, is on the Senate ballot for the first time, having been appointed last year to finish Marco Rubio’s term. She faces State Representative Angie Nixon, a progressive who won the Democratic primary in an upset.

Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, is seeking a second term in Georgia, a battleground that both parties this cycle initially considered the toughest for Democrats to hold onto. He is facing Representative Mike Collins, a Republican who won President Trump’s endorsement in the primary.

Senator Jim Risch, 83, a Republican, is heavily favored to win a fourth term in Idaho, a state President Trump carried by more than 36 percentage points in 2024. His toughest challenge comes from Todd Achilles, one of several independents challenging Republicans across the country this year.

Illinois’ open Senate seat, now held by retiring Senator Dick Durbin, a Democrat, is likely to remain blue. Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, a progressive, is favored to prevail over her Republican opponent, Don Tracy, a former chairman of the state Republican Party.

Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican, is vying to maintain party control of the seat held by retiring Senator Joni Ernst. Polls have shown her locked in a tight race against Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative, in a state that President Trump won three times.

Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican, is trying to survive an unexpectedly competitive race in deep-red Kansas. He faces Adam Hamilton, a centrist Democrat who has sought to corral farmers’ anger at economic conditions under President Trump.

Representative Andy Barr, a Republican, is running to succeed the retiring Senator Mitch McConnell, whose poor health came under scrutiny in recent months. Mr. Barr faces Charles Booker, a progressive former state lawmaker who has run for the Senate twice before.

Senator Bill Cassidy lost his Republican primary this year after President Trump targeted him for voting to convict him in his second impeachment trial. Now the seat Mr. Cassidy held for over a decade is up for grabs, and Representative Julia Letlow, who is backed by Mr. Trump, is heavily favored to win it over Jamie Davis, a Democratic farmer.
Senator Susan Collins, a Republican, is seeking a sixth term against the Democrat Troy Jackson in the toughest political environment she has faced over her 30-year career.

Senator Ed Markey, 80, a Democrat whose progressive bona fides helped him turn back a much younger challenger in the primary, is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. He faces John Deaton, a Republican lawyer and a Marine veteran.

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic former public health official, is in a competitive race against former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican who narrowly lost his Senate bid in 2024. The contest has become a key test for progressives, who are backing El-Sayed.

The race to replace the retiring Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat, pits the state’s lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, against Michele Tafoya, a sports journalist and a first-time candidate. The two have sparred over fraud in statewide programs and rising costs attributed to the Iran war and the Trump administration’s tariff policies.

Scott Colom, a Democratic prosecutor, has mounted an unexpectedly competitive challenge to Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a first-term Republican who has been reliably aligned with President Trump. While Ms. Hyde-Smith is still favored in conservative Mississippi, Mr. Colom would be the first Black senator elected from the state since Reconstruction.

A late withdrawal by the incumbent Republican, Steve Daines, left a Senate seat open in a historically conservative state. Kurt Alme, a Republican backed by President Trump, faces an unusually fractured field after national Democrats and state leaders shifted support toward an independent candidate, Seth Bodnar, instead of the Democrat who won the party’s primary, Alani Bankhead.

Dan Osborn, a mechanic, former union leader and military veteran running as an independent, is challenging Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican scion of an influential billionaire family with deep ties to Nebraska. To clear the way for Mr. Osborn’s bid, the Democratic primary winner, Cindy Burbank, declined the party’s nomination, potentially consolidating the anti-incumbent vote in the conservative stronghold.

Nearly 20 years ago, John E. Sununu, a Republican, lost his Senate seat to Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat. Now she is retiring, and Mr. Sununu is trying to make a comeback. He is facing Representative Chris Pappas, a low-key Democrat in his fourth term.
Senator Cory Booker, a Democrat and former Newark mayor elected to the Senate in 2013, faces Justin Murphy, a Republican attorney.

Senator Ben Ray Luján, a Democrat, is running for a second term in a solidly blue state against Larry E. Marker, a former oil and gas producer who won the Republican nomination as a write-in candidate.

Roy Cooper, the Democratic former North Carolina governor, and Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman, are competing to succeed Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who is retiring.

In one of the most expensive and consequential Senate races of this cycle, Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, is facing a challenge from Sherrod Brown, a Democrat. Mr. Brown lost his seat in 2024 after three terms in the Senate.

Markwayne Mullin left the Senate to become secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, and his replacement, Alan Armstrong, is ineligible to seek a full term under state law. Representative Kevin Hern, a Trump ally, is the clear favorite to win the open seat.
Senator Jeff Merkley is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. Among his challengers are State Senator David Brock Smith, a Republican, and Gary Lyndon Dye, a Libertarian.

Senator Jack Reed, a Democrat, is seeking a sixth term in a state that has not sent a Republican to the Senate since 2000. He is being challenged by Raymond McKay, a Republican activist who was formerly the network and telecommunications manager for the city of Warwick, R.I.

Senator Darline Graham, the Republican appointed to fill her deceased brother Lindsey Graham’s seat, is running for a full term of her own. Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat and a pediatrician, is hoping Ms. Graham’s inexperience and her ties to President Trump can help her flip a seat in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.

Senator Mike Rounds, a Republican, is running for a third term in one of the country’s most conservative states. Public polling has been limited, but some surveys have shown him in a closer-than-usual race with Brian Bengs, an independent. The Democratic nominee withdrew from the ballot.

Senator Bill Hagerty, a Trump-backed Republican, is seeking a second term in a state that President Trump won by nearly 30 points in 2024. His opponent, the Democratic environmental justice activist Marquita Bradshaw, previously ran for Senate in 2020 and 2024.

James Talarico, a state legislator, is trying to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to win a statewide election in Texas. He is facing Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general, in a race that is one of the most expensive American campaigns ever.
Senator Mark Warner, a Democrat, is seeking a fourth term in a state that is considered solidly blue. He faces Bert Mizusawa, a retired general who easily won the Republican primary.
Senator Shelley Moore Capito is running for a third term in West Virginia, a Republican stronghold. She faces Rachel Fetty Anderson, a lawyer and a Democratic former city councilwoman in Morgantown.

In deep-red Wyoming, the state’s lone at-large House member, Harriet Hageman, is favored to succeed Senator Cynthia Lummis, a Republican, who is retiring after serving one term. Ms. Hageman faces James Byrd, a Democratic former state lawmaker.

content.text: The mood at the watch party in Austin for Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas was livelier earlier, when an ‘80s cover band was performing, but when the band took a break, supporters of the Republican incumbent were refreshing election results on their phones, which show Abbott’s challenger, Gina Hinojosa, with an early lead with about 54 percent of the vote in.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, a Democrat, addressed a crowd of hundreds in downtown Atlanta after winning his re-election bid. “In sweeping and decisive victories,” he said, “the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed lame duck President Donald J. Trump.”

The Democrats have a greater than 95 percent chance to win the Senate, according to our estimates. A final call may not come for hours, but Democrats have either won or are likely to win the four Republican-held states they need to take the chamber: Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio. Democrats have additional opportunities in Kansas, Maine, Iowa and Alaska, where they are favored to prevail should another state fall through.

In the Kansas Senate race, Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate and megachurch pastor, has a lead with around 40 percent of the expected vote having been reported. While that advantage is expected to decrease as more votes are reported, Hamilton has greatly outperformed Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins statewide. Rural counties such as Ellis County, Labette County and Reno County have shifted close to 20 percentage points to the left.

A large number of votes are still to come in Johnson County, the largest in the state by population. The early vote there showed a large shift toward Hamilton, with the Democrat leading the county by 36 points.

One thing Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia won’t say as he congratulates Keisha Lance Bottoms for becoming the state’s Democratic governor-elect is that with his resounding Senate victory, he helped lift her and other Democrats down the ballot. Ossoff invited Bottoms to one of his big rallies as far back as May and also more recently, including to a rally that featured former President Barack Obama.

Democrats at the official watch party for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee are particularly excited about the fact that Representative Richard Hudson, Republican of North Carolina and the chairman of the National Republican Campaign Committee, is currently trailing his Democratic opponent.
North Carolina Ninth Congressional District Election Results ›

Virginia voters have approved a measure that restores the right to vote for people convicted of felonies upon their release, The Associated Press reported. The measure also limits the state’s ban on voting for people deemed mentally incompetent by a court, requiring that a court specifically finds that a person is unable to understand the act of voting.
James Talarico now has a 90 percent chance to win the
Senate race in Texas

for Democrats, according to our estimates. No Election Day vote has been counted yet, but his overwhelming advantage in the early vote means that his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, would need extraordinary turnout on Election Day to prevail.

David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for governor of Florida, just conceded. Addressing supporters in Tampa’s convention center, he said, “Yes, we have lost this election tonight, but we have not lost the fight in any of us.” He notes just how big of a night Democrats are having elsewhere. “This is a big night across the country,” he said, adding that “Americans are exercising the democracy that has been pent-up for a very long time.”

The Democrat Annie Andrews continues to lead in South Carolina, in part because she has managed to make strong inroads into blue-collar communities that have been strong supporters of President Trump.

Three South Carolina counties where white residents without college degrees make up a majority of the population have finished counting their votes. Each of those counties have shifted by more than 20 percentage points toward Andrews, compared with the 2024 presidential election.
More broadly, South Carolina counties that voted for Trump in 2024 swung to the left by an average of about 21 percentage points.
Virginia voters have approved a ballot measure repealing language in the state Constitution prohibiting marriage between same-sex couples, The Associated Press reported.

The ban has been unenforceable since the 2015 Supreme Court ruling that established same-sex marriage as a national right, but would come back into effect if that ruling were overturned. The measure establishes a right to marriage between consenting adults “regardless of sex, gender or race.”

In Jacksonville, Fla., Angie Nixon has just given a rousing concession speech in the Florida Senate race, in which she indicated she would not be fading into the background in state politics. “I’m an organizer, not a politician,” she said. “And organizers don’t quit on the mission because one option closes.” She added: “We have built something that no election outcome can take away from us.”

In South Carolina, Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee, has a chance to flip a Senate seat that has been held by a Republican since Strom Thurmond changed parties in 1964. She has done well throughout the state, shifting the vote more than 20 percentage points to the left in about a dozen counties that have largely completed reporting. She could also be the first woman ever elected to the U.S. Senate from the state, since Senator Darline Graham, her Republican opponent, was appointed to the seat.

content.text: In Texas, several heavily Hispanic counties across the state have reported a substantial share of their votes. James Talarico is running ahead of Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins in all of them. These include border counties in the Rio Grande Valley, like Cameron, which President Trump flipped in 2024, as well as urban counties like Bexar and El Paso, which Harris won in 2024 by much smaller margins.

Annie Andrews, a Democrat, is edging toward a stunning victory over Senator Darline Graham, a Republican, in the South Carolina Senate race, with a greater than 95 percent chance to win, according to our estimates. This is not a projection, but an Andrews victory would greatly narrow the Republican path to retaining control of the Senate.
The mood inside President Trump’s watch event in the East Room is fairly lackluster and devoid of energy, according to people on hand.

Trump’s history of election night events in that room is not stellar: In 2018, he huddled with Mike Pence’s adviser Nick Ayers, who the president wanted to make his own White House chief of staff, before Ayers turned it down. That night, several high-profile Republican elected officials stayed away from the White House. And 2020 was marked by the president’s infamous declaration that “frankly, we did win” the election, after Arizona was called for President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

Sherrod Brown, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Ohio, lost his 2024 re-election by just three percentage points. In his bid to return to the Senate, he has improved on his margins in the handful of completed counties by a large margin. Many of them are still redder than in 2018, though, which was the last time Brown won statewide.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City delivered a speech contrasting the despair he felt as a Democrat watching the presidential results roll in in 2024 with the hope he feels tonight.

“We have begun the work of transforming our party and making it belong to the working people once again,” Mamdani said from Gov. Kathy Hochul’s victory party at a Hilton in Midtown Manhattan, adding: “For too long in this country and frankly even across our state, politics has been treated like a game. We track who’s up, who’s down, we pore over palace intrigue and relegate the issues that affect the working class to the margins.”

Democrats’ win in Florida’s 22nd Congressional District is their third in the state in a district that Republican state lawmakers redrew this year to favor their party. It suggests that Republicans’ strategy to use unusual mid-decade redistricting to try to hold on to House control is falling flat.
Florida 22nd Congressional District Election Results ›

Supporters of Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic state lawmaker running for governor of Texas, are optimistic an hour after most polls closed in Texas. They hope she denies the sitting governor, Greg Abbott, a record fourth term. A victory for Hinojosa would mean the state’s first Hispanic governor and the first Democrat in more than three decades.

Jaime Harrison, the Democrat who lost the South Carolina Senate race six years ago, has taken the stage at Dr. Annie Andrews’s election night party in Charleston. The race is still too close to call, but he is praising Andrews for the long campaign she has waged for the seat. “It’s time that we bring hope back to South Carolina,” he said. “It’s time that we have someone that represents us and not just the lobbyists and the corporate interests.”

I just spoke with Representative Ralph Norman, the South Carolina Republican who lost in the Senate primary to Senator Darline Graham, who is currently in a closer-than-expected race in South Carolina despite being backed by President Trump.

“I think they say pride goeth before the fall, and we’re seeing that all across the country,” Norman said of Trump. “You can’t force a person on South Carolina,” he added. “And that’s pretty evident now.”

In the Texas Senate race, James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, is doing well in the area around Dallas. He is leading Ken Paxton by 13 percentage points in Collin County, with roughly 80 percent of the expected vote reported. And in nearby Denton County, Talarico is leading by about nine points.

Paxton, whom President Trump endorsed in the primary against the incumbent, Senator John Cornyn, has deep ties to these counties, both of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024. Paxton used to live in Collin County and moved to Denton after his divorce.

If the Democrats’ apparent strength in the South holds tonight, it could expand the map to even redder targets that have yet to report their votes. In Mississippi, for instance, just one county has completed the vote count thus far — Jasper, a heavily Black rural county — swinging about 19 points to the left from the 2024 presidential election. If shifts like that occur in the rest of the state, Republicans could have a race on their hands.
Chris Pappas,
the first openly gay man
in U.S. history to win a Senate seat, gave a jubilant victory speech at the Puritan Backroom, his family’s restaurant, shortly after his Republican rival, John E. Sununu, conceded the race.
Pappas thanked his family, parents, and “the man standing next me, my amazing husband, Vann.” The crowded room let out a long cheer. Pappas, who
spoke little of his history-making potential
during the campaign, joked that “apparently the wrong man” was on the ballot today.
“Love and truth prevail tonight,” he said.

The White House just released President Trump’s schedule for tomorrow, and as of now, he has no public events. The schedule says he has four policy meetings at the White House, but they are all closed to the press.

In Texas, James Talarico is outperforming Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 margins in nearly every county that has reported results. Often used as a comparison point for Talarico, O’Rourke, the 2018 Democratic nominee for Senate, had come closer than any recent Democrat to flipping Texas, losing to Ted Cruz by less than three percentage points.

Counting is still underway throughout the state, and the picture could change as more Election Day votes arrive. But currently Talarico is outperforming O’Rourke by double digits in multiple counties, and our election forecast is leaning in his direction.
Jamie Ager,
a Democratic farmer in western North Carolina
, has flipped the heavily conservative district encompassing rural mountain towns.

The state’s 11th Congressional District was not supposed to be this competitive for Democrats, even with the liberal bubble of Asheville growing. But Ager’s victory has come to exemplify two trends of the 2026 midterms: Candidate quality still matters, and many rural areas appear to be more competitive.
Phil Weiser, the Democratic attorney general of Colorado, easily won a contest to become the state’s next governor, The Associated Press reported.

The race was never that close in solidly blue Colorado, and the gap widened when many prominent Republicans refused to back their party’s nominee, Victor Marx, a ministry leader and martial arts expert who made many hard-to-verify claims about his past.
In the 2024 Nebraska Senate race, Dan Osborn
outran

Kamala Harris in 91 of the state’s 93 counties but ultimately lost by about seven percentage points. This time, he will need to do even better in his bid to challenge Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent, who has the advantage in rural counties across the rest of the state.
Osborn is expected to do well in three counties that will account for over half of the statewide vote:
Douglas
, which contains Omaha;
Sarpy
, Omaha’s southern suburbs; and
Lancaster
, which includes Lincoln. He is seeking to outperform his 2024 margins in these areas, while cutting into Ricketts’s lead in smaller counties. Other noteworthy counties include
Dakota
, which Osborn nearly won in 2024, and
Colfax
, where he outperformed Harris by 18 points. Both have meatpacking plants and a high share of Hispanic residents, and they could offer indications of how well his populist platform is landing.

Democrats have now flipped their first House seat of the night with their victory in a congressional district in western North Carolina, a mostly conservative area that had shifted to the left in recent elections. Even before Representative Chuck Edwards, the Republican incumbent, ended his re-election bid in the face of a harassment scandal, his seat had been expected to be competitive.

content.text: The excitement is building here at James Talarico’s watch party, where thousands are glued to a huge screen, the skyline of Austin in the background, cheering loudly at each mention of the Texas race. “I’m jubilant,” said Rafael Anchia, a two-decade veteran of the State Legislature.

Jamie Ager, a Democrat and fourth-generation farmer, defeated Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican state legislator, in a House race in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, according to The Associated Press, flipping a seat held by a Republican leaving office in the face of misconduct accusations. It was the first House seat flip for Democrats.

Representative Chuck Edwards dropped his re-election bid in August after a House panel found that he had “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct” toward two female staffers. Balkcom was picked to replace him on the ticket, giving her a short period to make her case to voters in the sprawling district, a mostly conservative region in the western part of the state anchored by a liberal city, Asheville. The district supported President Trump by about 10 percentage points in 2024.
North Carolina 11th Congressional District Election Results ›

Roy Cooper said at his watch party that “tonight, we told Washington loud and clear that North Carolinians will always matter more than the billionaires and the insiders.” His campaign was premised on the slogan “make stuff cost less,” which resonated widely in a rapidly growing state that still has large pockets of rural communities from the mountains out west to the beach towns in the east.
“I am still a prisoner of hope,” Cooper said, adding that voters were clearly eager for a course correction.

Once a reliable swing state that tilted slightly to the left, Iowa has been all but out of reach for Democrats in recent years. If Josh Turek hopes to compete against Representative Ashley Hinson for the state’s open Senate seat, he’ll want to keep things close in
Pottawattamie County

. That county includes his hometown, Council Bluffs, but President Trump won it by about 20 percentage points in 2024. Turek will also want to improve significantly on Kamala Harris’s 10-point margin in
Polk County
, the largest in the state.
Hinson, for her part, will hope for a respectable showing in the Democratic-leaning
Linn County
, which is in her district. She was also a well-known news anchor in Cedar Rapids, the county seat, for more than a decade.
It didn’t get as much attention as his spending in the Texas Senate race, but Elon Musk’s fingerprints have been all over the Texas governor’s race, too.

Musk gave $5 million to try to help Greg Abbott’s re-election bid in September. Abbott had a vaunted fund-raising operation and held an advantage on advertising spending of about five to one over the Democratic nominee, Gina Hinojosa.

Some of the most strongly Democratic shifts in the Senate races tonight are occurring in ancestrally Democratic counties in Appalachia — from mountainous counties in Virginia, like Norton, Wise and Buchanan, to eastern coal counties in Kentucky like Breathitt and Floyd. These are areas where the Democratic Party had lost the most ground over the last few decades.
Roy Cooper declares at his watch party in downtown Raleigh, N.C., that voters have resoundingly made their voices heard. He came onstage to cheers of “Cooper! Cooper!”

In South Carolina, Annie Andrews is leading Darline Graham, the Republican incumbent, with around half the vote counted so far in the Senate race. While many of the state’s larger counties have reported around half their results, Richland County, home to the city of Columbia, has not reported any yet. Richland could be a strong source of votes for Andrews, as Kamala Harris won the county by 35 percentage points in 2024. In a typically red state that Democrats are looking to flip, our election forecast is leaning in Andrews’s direction.

The results in Texas are still uncertain. If James Talarico beats Ken Paxton, it would be a significant moment in the state, but it would also be the result of something close to a perfect storm of events. If Gina Hinojosa wins the governor’s race for Democrats, that would say significantly more about the change in the state and across the country that is happening right now.

Senator Ashley Moody, a Republican, has won the special election in Florida to complete Marco Rubio’s term. Republicans expected to cruise in her race. But Angie Nixon’s shocking win in the Democratic Senate primary reshaped the contours of the race and turned it into a real contest. Moody hung on despite waging something of a quiet campaign. Her winning margin will be much narrower than that of other recent Florida Republican Senate candidates.

The Florida Senate bid by Angie Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, was viewed as a test case for the left’s theory that they could win in battleground areas. She fell short against Ashley Moody, but her strong showing is still likely to be viewed as a positive sign by progressives.

Another race I’m tracking in Texas is the usually little-watched election for the Texas Railroad Commission, the state’s oil and gas regulatory body. Jon Rosenthal, the Democrat and an oil and gas engineer from Houston, is up against Bo French, a former Republican county chairman whose family owns an oil and gas company. This fall, French
drew blowback
for racist social media posts and comments.
According to the White House pool report, President Trump is watching returns in the East Room with some of his cabinet members and advisers.

Senate Republicans had hoped to grab a Democratic-held seat in New Hampshire to offset potential losses elsewhere. They believed former Senator John Sununu had a path to do so given the political power of the family name and his previous tenure in the Senate.

Democrats always thought that would be a heavy lift, considering that the state voted Democratic in recent presidential elections. They proved to be correct, easing concerns that the party could lose on friendly territory in these midterms.

It can be easy to overlook former Gov. Roy Cooper’s victory in North Carolina’s Senate race because Republicans abandoned the race weeks ago. But Cooper is the first Democrat to win a Senate race there since 2008, and the state has repeatedly broken the hopeful hearts of Democrats in Senate races since then.

In the South Carolina Senate race, Annie Andrews is outperforming Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins by double digits in three counties where results are essentially complete. These areas vary greatly from one another in terms of demographics: Lee County is majority Black and Kamala Harris won it by 18 percentage points in 2024, while Barnwell and McCormick counties are predominantly white regions that President Trump won.
